title: How to Foam Roll: Areas, Timing and a 10-Minute Routine — cv.cm
description: How to foam roll step by step: roller density, calves, hamstrings, quads, glutes, outer thigh and upper back, 20–30 s pauses, and a timed 10-minute routine.
h1: How do you foam roll correctly?
answer: Place the roller under a large muscle, support part of your weight with your hands or other leg, and roll slowly, about 2–3 cm per second, for 30–60 seconds per area. Pause 20–30 seconds on a tender spot. Keep pressure firm but not painful. Roll the calves, thighs, buttocks and upper back, but not the lower back or neck.

sections.h: What foam rolling is and what it is not
body: Foam rolling is a form of self-massage. You lie or sit on a firm foam cylinder and use your body weight to press and roll a muscle over it. It is often called self-myofascial release. Many people use it to loosen up before exercise or to feel less stiff afterward.

The name "release" suggests that rolling stretches or breaks up the connective tissue (fascia) around muscles. That is not what happens. A 2008 modeling study estimated that changing thick fascia, such as the band along the outer thigh, by even 1% would need forces far beyond anything a person can apply with a hand or roller. The short-term effects people feel are more likely due to changes in how the nervous system senses stretch and pressure.
This guide is for healthy adults. It is not medical advice, and it is not a way to treat an injury.

body: If you are not sure, start with a smooth medium or soft roller about 15 cm across. You can always add pressure by shifting more weight onto it.

ol: Set the roller on a firm floor or a mat. Wear clothes that do not bunch up.
Place the muscle on the roller and take part of your weight on your hands, forearms or the other foot.
Roll slowly, about 2–3 cm per second, from one end of the muscle to the other. One pass takes about 10 seconds.
When you find a tender spot, stop and rest on it for 20–30 seconds while you breathe slowly. Let the muscle relax.
Spend 30–60 seconds on each area, and no more than about 2 minutes on any one muscle in a session.
Stay on muscle. Lift off before the roller reaches a joint such as the knee, hip bone or ankle.

body: Pressure in words: light means most of your weight is on your hands; medium means about half your weight is on the roller; firm means most of your weight is on it. Aim for 4–6 out of 10. Discomfort that feels good is fine. Sharp, burning or tingling pain, or pain that makes you hold your breath, means ease off or stop.
To make it easier, put more weight on your hands or use both legs on the roller. To make it harder, cross one leg over the other or use a firmer roller.

sections.h: The main areas, one by one

ul: Calves: sit with the roller under one calf, hands on the floor behind you. Roll from just above the ankle to just below the back of the knee, and stop before the knee crease. Turn the leg in and out to reach the inner and outer parts. Cross the other leg on top for more pressure.

Hamstrings (back of the thigh): sit with the roller under the back of the thighs, hands behind you. Roll from just above the back of the knee to just below the buttock crease. Do not roll the back of the knee itself.

Quadriceps (front of the thigh): lie face down on your forearms, roller under the front of the thighs. Roll from just above the kneecap to just below the hip crease. Keep your stomach and buttocks lightly tensed so the lower back does not sag.

Glutes (buttocks): sit on the roller, cross one ankle over the other knee, and lean toward the side of the crossed leg. Roll a short distance over the fleshy part of the buttock. Stay off the tailbone.

Outer thigh (the IT band side): lie on your side with the roller under the outer thigh, between the hip and the knee, with the top leg crossed in front and its foot on the floor for support. Roll slowly and lightly. This area is often very tender. Rolling cannot lengthen or "release" the IT band, which is a tough strip of connective tissue. Many people get more comfort by rolling the front of the thigh and the buttock muscles instead.

Upper back: lie on your back with the roller across the upper back, below the shoulder blades, knees bent and feet flat. Cross your arms over your chest or support your head with your hands. Lift your hips slightly and roll from the middle of the back up to the top of the shoulder blades. Do not roll up onto the neck or down onto the lower back.

body: Use this routine after a walk, run or workout, or on a rest day. Time each step with a timer, for example cv.cm's countdown.

body: Before exercise, a shorter version is enough: 30 seconds on each muscle you are about to use, followed by your usual warm-up such as easy jogging or dynamic movement. Long, heavy rolling right before a sport is not needed.
Daily rolling is fine for most people at medium pressure. If an area is still tender the next day, halve the pressure and time for that area.
Foam rolling has been studied more than most self-massage tools, mostly in young, healthy and active adults. The effects are real but small and short-lived.

ul: Range of motion: a 2020 review of 26 trials found that foam rolling gave a short-term increase in joint range of motion compared with doing nothing, about as much as stretching, but not more.

Performance and soreness: a 2019 review of 21 studies found that rolling before exercise gave very small gains in sprint speed and flexibility, and rolling after exercise slightly reduced how sore muscles felt. The authors called the effects rather minor and partly negligible.
There is little evidence that foam rolling prevents injury, and none that it removes toxins, breaks down scar tissue, or reshapes the body.

body: A fair summary: foam rolling may help you feel looser and a little less sore for a short time. If you enjoy it, it is a reasonable part of a warm-up or cool-down.

sections.h: Safety: what to avoid and when to stop

ul: Do not roll the lower back on a roller. There are no ribs to protect it, and your weight presses on the spine and its joints. For lower back muscles, lie on your back with knees bent and do gentle knee-to-chest movements instead, or use a soft ball against a wall beside the spine, not on it.
Do not roll the neck, the front of the hip, the back of the knee, or directly on joints and bones such as the kneecap, hip bone or ankle.
Do not roll over bruises, a fresh injury, a torn muscle, broken skin, varicose veins, or areas that are numb.
Never roll a calf that is swollen, warm, red or painful, especially after a long flight, surgery or illness. It can be a blood clot. Get medical help the same day.

Ask a doctor or physical therapist first if you have osteoporosis, a recent fracture or surgery, a history of blood clots, a bleeding disorder or take blood thinners, diabetes with numb feet, or are pregnant.
Getting down to and up from the floor can be hard for some older adults. Rolling against a wall while standing is a gentler option.

body: Stop and see a doctor if rolling causes sharp pain, pain that lasts more than a few days, bruising, or numbness or tingling down an arm or leg. Pain that wakes you at night or comes with swelling or fever also needs a medical check.

ul: Rolling too fast: you just slide back and forth. Fix: about 10 seconds per pass, and pause on tender spots.
Too much pressure on day one: you are sore the next day. Fix: halve the pressure and the time, and take more weight on your hands.
Staying on one spot for minutes: it gets more tender, not less. Fix: 20–30 seconds, then move on.
Rolling onto the lower back or neck: strain on the spine. Fix: stop the upper back roll at the bottom of the shoulder blades.
Holding your breath: the muscle tenses. Fix: breathe slowly and let your body sink onto the roller.

faq.q: Is it better to foam roll before or after a workout?
faq.a: Both are fine. Before exercise, keep it short, about 30 seconds per muscle, and follow it with a normal warm-up. After exercise, a longer 10-minute routine may help you feel less sore.

faq.q: How long should you foam roll each muscle?
faq.a: About 30–60 seconds per area, with 20–30 second pauses on tender spots. Most people do not need more than 2 minutes on any one muscle.

faq.q: Why does foam rolling hurt so much?
faq.a: You may be using a roller that is too firm or putting too much weight on it. Take more weight on your hands or switch to a softer roller; it should feel firm, not painful.

faq.q: Can foam rolling get rid of cellulite?
faq.a: No. Foam rolling does not remove cellulite or fat. Any change in how the skin looks after rolling is temporary.

faq.q: Should you foam roll your IT band?
faq.a: You can roll the outer thigh lightly if it feels good, but it will not lengthen or release the band. Rolling the front of the thigh and the buttocks is often more comfortable.
